title: If not true, don't
hookLine: if it isn't right, don't do it; if it isn't true, don't say it (Meditations 12.17)

lines: A RULE FOR HANDS AND MOUTH.
cards: "Love the haircut." "Running five minutes late," sent from the couch. "No, it's fine, really."
Most small untruths in a day are soft, quick, and meant to keep things moving. Nobody keeps count.
In the last book of his notebook, Marcus writes himself a rule short enough for a sticky note, with two halves: one about your hands, one about your mouth.

teach.h: TWO GATES: IS IT RIGHT? IS IT TRUE?
teach.b: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: "If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it." First, the shape. It's not a lecture on honesty.
It's a filter with two gates. Before an act: is it right? Before a word: is it true?
If the answer is no, you don't need a long debate. You just don't. Second, the Greek.
The word for true is alēthes, from the family of alētheia, truth. Truth runs all through the notebook.
In book three Marcus put it among his four great goods, and in book nine he calls the deliberate lie a kind of impiety, a wrong against nature itself, which he says is also rightly called truth.
A lie, even a small one, is a mind saying something it knows isn't so. Third, what the rule doesn't say. It doesn't say: say every true thing.
Marcus elsewhere tells himself to be kind, to correct people gently, to keep quiet when quiet is better.

teach.h: ALĒTHES: THE GREEK WORD FOR TRUE.
teach.b: Between the untrue word and the cruel true word, there's a third door: silence, or a smaller true thing.

teach.h: NOT EVERY TRUE THING NEEDS SAYING.
teach.b: "I'm not sure about the haircut, but you look happy" is true. So is "I'm still on the couch, leaving now." Fourth, why it's at the end.

teach.h: A RULE LIGHT ENOUGH TO PACK.
teach.b: To many readers, book twelve reads like a man packing for a trip, keeping what's light and what matters.
A two-gate rule is the kind of thing you pack.

how: Readers of the Meditations often treat 12.17 as a daily check, pausing before an act or a word to ask whether it is right and whether it is true.

o: two doors Romans kept open for guests and strangers
Marcus's two checks: is the act right, is the word true
two ways to hide a lie so that nobody can catch it

s: Marcus's rule means you must say every true thing you think
the rule is about what never to say; elsewhere he tells himself to be kind and gentle.
the rule comes from book twelve, the last book of the Meditations
it's 12.17, near the end of the notebook.
the rule has two halves, one for actions and one for words
if it is not right, don't do it; if it is not true, don't say it.

games.q: a friend asks if you like their new haircut. you don't, much. by Marcus's rule, what's open to you?
o: a smaller true thing, like "you look happy with it."
a full list of what's wrong with it.
games.why: the rule closes the door on the untrue word, but it doesn't require every true thing. a smaller true thing, or silence, still fits.

practice: Think back over yesterday and find one small untrue thing you said, a polite fib, a softened excuse, an "I'm fine," and just look at it, without scolding.
Then picture the same moment again, and find the smaller true thing you could have said, or the silence that would have done.

wordCard.voice: Two gates. Marcus's rule has one for acts, is it right, and one for words, is it true; if not, don't. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: true. The word Marcus uses in 12.17: if it is not true, do not say it.

carryVoice: Your line: a smaller true thing. Silence counts as an honest answer, too. See you tomorrow.
